prompt: Where does the section say Domain-Driven Design earns its cost?

choices.text: Wherever there is a database
choices.why: The phone-number page has a database and is better as plain CRUD.

choices.text: Where the hard part is rules that interact
choices.why: Right. Lending's rules are each simple; the trouble is where they meet.

choices.text: In systems that have to handle a very high volume of requests
choices.why: Throughput is listed among the difficulties DDD has little to offer for.

choices.text: In a short prototype, to get the design right from the start
choices.why: A system that lives for a campaign is in the "probably not" column.

prompt: A team has entities/, value_objects/ and repositories/ folders but never talks to the librarians. What does the section say they have?

choices.text: Complete DDD, since the folders follow the book
choices.why: The folders are the tactical half; the section calls the strategic half the larger one.

choices.text: Strategic DDD without the tactical patterns
choices.why: It is the other way round: the folders are tactical, and the conversations are what is missing.

choices.text: The tactical half only, and possibly the same tangle in more files
choices.why: Right. Without agreed words and boundaries, the patterns rearrange the problem without solving it.

prompt: Which of these are signs, from the section's table, that DDD is probably worth it? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Only people outside the team can explain the rules
choices.why: Right. The knowledge is in the business, and the code has to learn its words.

choices.text: The rules change every few months, after arguments
choices.why: Right. A model in the business's words is what makes those changes cheap.

choices.text: The hardest part is the screens
choices.why: Screens are in the "probably not" column.

choices.text: The system will live for years
choices.why: Right. The conversations pay back over a long life.

prompt: Why does the section object to code that writes r["st"] = 4 for a lapsed hold?

choices.text: Every conversation then goes through someone who knows what 4 means
choices.why: Right. Translation is where meaning leaks, as the status 5 story shows.

choices.text: A dictionary lookup is slower than reading an attribute on an object
choices.why: Speed never comes up; the cost is in understanding.

choices.text: Python forbids numbers as status values
choices.why: Python allows it; the objection is about language, not the interpreter.

prompt: In holds.py, a copy is shelved on 3 June 2026. On which day of June does has_lapsed first answer True?
hint: The deadline itself is still allowed.

prompt: The librarians coin a name, in a meeting, for giving a lapsed hold one more day. What does the section recommend for the code?

choices.text: A flag named retry_lapsed, so the code stays technical and the business words stay out of it
choices.why: That is the section's example of how the two languages drift apart again.

choices.text: Nothing until the glossary is approved by everyone, in a later release
choices.why: The section asks for the rename in the same week, while the word is fresh.

choices.text: A second_chance method, a test named after it, and the word in the glossary
choices.why: Right. The language changed, so the code changes with it.

prompt: Which of the library's subdomains does the section call core?

choices.text: Card and Pix payments, because money is involved
choices.why: Payments are generic: every organisation has them and providers do them better.

choices.text: The catalogue, because it holds the most data
choices.why: Size does not decide it; the catalogue is supporting, the same work every library does.

choices.text: Lending
choices.why: Right. Its rules are what the library decides about itself and why members come.

choices.text: Acquisitions, because buying books is how the collection grows
choices.why: A few orders a month: supporting, and small.

prompt: The library wants to write its own handling of card payments for fines. What does the section say about that?

choices.text: Effort spent on a generic subdomain, done worse than by a provider
choices.why: Right. Generic means somebody else's core.

choices.text: Good practice, because fines are part of lending, the core
choices.why: The fine rules are core; taking the payment is not.

choices.text: Acceptable as long as it uses every pattern of lesson 12
choices.why: More care on the wrong subdomain is still care in the wrong place.

prompt: The city offers every library a shared catalogue for free. What happens to the library's catalogue subdomain?

choices.text: It becomes core, because the library must now integrate with the city
choices.why: Integration work does not make a subdomain a differentiator.

choices.text: It becomes generic, and adopting the city's is the right move
choices.why: Right. Somebody now does it well for everyone, so it leaves the library's own care.

choices.text: Nothing, since subdomains are fixed once they are sorted
choices.why: The section has a part called "Subdomains move" for this case.

choices.text: It splits into two bounded contexts
choices.why: Contexts are the solution side; the question is about what kind of problem it is now.

prompt: In tour.py, what connects acquisitions.Book, catalogue.Book and lending.Book?

choices.text: A shared parent class Book that all three inherit from
choices.why: There is no shared class at all; that would be the enterprise model again.

choices.text: The ISBN string they all carry, nothing else
choices.why: Right. The last line prints one ISBN for all three.

choices.text: The title, same in every context
choices.why: Only the catalogue's Book has a title; the others never mention it.

prompt: A developer proposes renaming lending.Book to Copy, since it is really a copy. What does the section say?

choices.text: Yes, because a word should mean the same thing across the whole library
choices.why: That is the one-model belief; inside lending, "book" is the desk's own word.

choices.text: No: the lending desk calls it a book, and lending's code should speak the desk's language
choices.why: Right. A bounded context lets each meaning keep its own word.

choices.text: Yes, but only if the catalogue renames its class to Work at the same time
choices.why: That couples two contexts' naming, which the boundary exists to avoid.

prompt: Match each language to its usual boundary for a context inside one program.

pairs.right: an internal/ directory the compiler protects
a module-info.java that exports one package
a package exposing what its __init__.py lists
a folder others reach through one index.ts

prompt: Match each relationship on the library's map to the pair it joins.
Lending uses the payment provider's own names for payment states. Why does the section call that acceptable?

choices.text: Because a downstream must always adopt the upstream's model
choices.why: The catalogue does the opposite with the bibliographic service; conforming is a choice.

choices.text: The provider will not change for one library, and its model is reasonable
choices.why: Right. Conforming to a good model saves a translation nobody needs.

choices.text: Because payments are core, so lending must own them
choices.why: Payments are generic, and owning them is exactly what lending avoids.

choices.text: Because the two teams plan their releases together
choices.why: That would be a partnership; the library is one customer among thousands.

prompt: The shared ISBN kernel between catalogue and acquisitions grows a Book class "to save duplication". What has happened?

choices.text: The kernel has become the one enterprise model again
choices.why: Right. A shared kernel works while it stays small; a shared Book is what the contexts were drawn to avoid.

choices.text: Nothing important; a shared kernel can hold any code both teams use
choices.why: Every addition needs both teams to agree, so a large kernel couples them on everything.

choices.text: The relationship has turned into an anticorruption layer
choices.why: An ACL translates between two models; this merged them.

prompt: In the ddd-strategic directory, which file is the only one that names the service's fields, such as ttl and aut?

choices.text: catalogue.py
choices.why: catalogue.py knows only its own Book; it has never heard of the feed.

choices.text: acl.py
choices.why: Right. When the service renames a field, one file changes.

choices.text: tour.py
choices.why: tour.py walks one title through the three contexts and never sees the feed.

prompt: The fourth record has status D. Why does acl.py refuse it instead of adding a withdrawn flag to Book?

choices.text: Python dataclasses cannot hold a boolean field
choices.why: They can; the choice is about the model, not the tool.

choices.text: Because the service will send the record again later with status A
choices.why: Nothing says it will; withdrawn means withdrawn.

choices.text: A flag would bring a concept the catalogue does not need into its model
choices.why: Right. The layer decides what is not accepted, and keeps the inside simpler.

prompt: A new upstream, the city's events calendar, sends JSON whose fields already match the library's model almost exactly, and it is happy to take requests. What fits?

choices.text: An anticorruption layer, because every external model must be translated
choices.why: A layer is for an upstream that will not change and would damage your model; this one fails both tests.

choices.text: Customer/supplier, or conforming, without a layer
choices.why: Right. The model is close and the upstream listens, so translation would be code for nothing.

choices.text: Separate ways, because external data is never worth integrating
choices.why: Separate ways fits when connecting costs more than it gives; nothing here says so.

prompt: Put the steps of a first event-storming session in the order the section gives.
items: Everybody writes orange events at once
The room arranges them into one timeline
Pink notes mark disagreements and questions
Commands, actors and policies are added
Lines are drawn where the language changes
trap: Drawing boundaries first would decide the model before the wall has shown where the words change.

prompt: An orange note is a domain event, written in the ___ tense, such as "Hold lapsed".
On the wall, the notes change from "Copy received" to "Title catalogued" to "Hold placed", and the people saying them change too. What is that evidence of?

choices.text: Three subdomains that must all be core
choices.why: Whether a part is core is a question of difference; the wall shows where words change.

choices.text: Candidate boundaries between bounded contexts
choices.why: Right. The library's three contexts came off exactly those shifts.

choices.text: Inconsistent naming that a glossary should merge into one word
choices.why: Different words for different work are the point; merging them builds the one enterprise model.

choices.text: A missing anticorruption layer between the three teams
choices.why: An ACL is chosen per relationship later; the wall first finds the contexts.

prompt: The bibliographic service starts sending authors as "Given Surname" instead of "SURNAME, Given". Which code in the library has to change?

choices.text: catalogue.py, the search, the desk screen and the overdue letters
choices.why: That would be the case without a layer; with one, none of them ever saw the service's format.

choices.text: Nothing, because author() already handles every format
choices.why: author() splits on ", " and would title-case the whole name; it handles their old format.

choices.text: Only the author function in acl.py
choices.why: Right. The translation of their format lives in one place.
